report:
Short answer
- The finetuning pushed the model toward a generic/high-frequency unigram bias: Model B is slightly more likely to emit very common short tokens (space-prefixed letters, "is", "it", "\n", "in", " a", etc.) than A.
- Mechanistically this looks like a small, broadly distributed additive bias (not a structured change in late-layers), i.e., a nearly uniform shift that increases probability mass on frequent tokens.

Why (evidence → conclusion)
1. Difference norms are essentially zero everywhere
   - The L2 norms by (layer, position) are near-zero across the board. That indicates the finetuning did not create a large, localized representational feature in particular layers/positions; instead the change is very small and diffuse. That pattern is consistent with a global additive bias (a tiny logit shift) rather than creation of a new high-level feature or attention/transformer-sublayer effect.

2. Logit-lens directions point to very common tokens
   - The top tokens that the difference vectors point at are the same across many (layer, position) cells and are all very common short tokens: space+letter tokens like " o", very frequent function words ("is", "it", "in", " a", "or", "s"), newline, and short letter tokens (" p", " t"). That is exactly what you would expect if the residual-change is pushing logits toward the high-frequency part of the vocabulary (a unigram-like bias).

3. Patchscope readouts are uninformative
   - Injecting the difference into identity prompts produced no strong, semantically coherent continuations (the readouts are essentially blank/weak). That again supports the idea that the change is a small global logit bias rather than a new pattern that meaningfully changes generation behavior in context-sensitive ways.

Plausible finetuning objectives that explain this pattern
- Training that encourages higher entropy / more generic outputs (e.g., label smoothing, KL-regularization toward a unigram distribution, or finetuning on a dataset made of very common tokens) would produce exactly this shift: small, broad increases in probability for frequent tokens.
- Similarly, an objective that penalizes rarer or riskier tokens (making outputs "safer" or more conservative) would produce the same effect.

Confidence and alternative explanations
- Confidence: moderate. The signals strongly indicate a generic/common-token bias, and the diffuse, small-magnitude change points to an additive logit-style effect rather than a structural behavioral change.
- Alternatives: the finetuning dataset could simply have been dominated by very short/common-token text (so MLE on that data would produce the same shift). But the net functional interpretation remains a move toward high-frequency/unigram outputs.

Conclusion
- The finetuning objective was to bias the model toward producing high-frequency/common tokens (i.e., a unigram/high-entropy or “safer/generic” output objective), implemented as a small, global additive shift in logit-space.
